The West Australian dhufish Glaucosoma hebraicum is a large-bodied, long-lived serranid endemic to the continental shelf waters of southwestern Australia. Newly hatched larvae emerge from pelagic eggs with a yolk sac and an initial body mass of just 0.001 grams [Wwb = 0.001 grams], a value derived from the calculated volume of a 1.25 millimeter diameter egg. This extremely small neonatal mass reflects the high fecundity typical of broadcast-spawning marine teleosts and places the species at the lower end of the size spectrum for its family. Following the transition to exogenous feeding, the planktonic larvae undergo a pelagic larval phase that can last several weeks before settlement. During the early juvenile period, growth is rapid as individuals exploit the abundant benthic invertebrate fauna of rocky reefs. Field surveys and otolith-based growth studies have revealed that this species attains an ultimate standard length of 98.1 centimeters [Li = 98.1 centimeters], a substantial size that positions it as one of the larger predatory fishes within its temperate reef ecosystem.

Sexual maturation in the West Australian dhufish occurs at a relatively small body size compared to its ultimate dimensions, a pattern that appears to be associated with its extended reproductive lifespan. Puberty is reached at a standard length of 30.1 centimeters [Lp = 30.1 centimeters], a value estimated from morphometric relationships established for the congeneric species Glaucosoma scapulare and consistent with the onset of gonad development observed in field-caught specimens. The corresponding wet weight at puberty, calculated on the basis of the length-weight relationship for the species, is 442 grams [Wwp = 442 grams]. This early maturation relative to maximum size suggests an opportunistic life-history strategy in which reproductive output begins well before somatic growth is complete, allowing individuals to contribute to the population over many years. The transition to adulthood is marked by vitellogenesis in females and spermiation in males, with gonadal recrudescence occurring each austral winter in preparation for the spawning season.

The reproductive biology of Glaucosoma hebraicum is characterised by a moderately high daily reproductive output, which is directly linked to water temperature during the spawning season. At the thermal regime typical of the species' primary spawning grounds along the lower west coast of Australia (20.4 °C [T = 20.4 °C]), females release approximately 3 million eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = approximately 3 million eggs per spawning event], and they typically complete one such spawning event per year [F_R_i = one such spawning event per year]. This fecundity level is consistent with that of other large serranid fishes and reflects the substantial energetic investment that females channel into gamete production over a compressed annual window. The eggs are pelagic and buoyant, dispersing widely with oceanic currents before hatching. The reproductive season itself is relatively brief, with most spawning activity concentrated in the warmer months between November and March, when surface temperatures are highest and primary productivity supports larval food availability.

The ultimate body mass attained by adult West Australian dhufish is substantial, underscoring the species' position as a top predator within its demersal community. The largest individuals recorded from commercial and recreational catches can reach a maximum wet weight of 15,300 grams [Wwi = 15,300 grams], equivalent to 15.3 kilograms. Such large specimens are typically older females, reflecting the pronounced sexual size dimorphism observed in this species. The attainment of this ultimate wet weight is a gradual process that spans many years, with growth rates decelerating markedly after the onset of sexual maturity as energetic resources are increasingly diverted toward annual reproductive effort. Comparative studies with other large-bodied serranids, such as the hapuku (Polyprion oxygeneios), indicate that the dhufish exhibits a moderately slow growth trajectory consistent with its extended lifespan and late age at maximum size.

Longevity is a defining feature of the life history of the West Australian dhufish, with the species ranking among the longer-lived teleosts of the temperate Australian continental shelf. In the waters off the coast of Western Australia, where mean annual sea surface temperatures average 20.4 °C [T = 20.4 °C], the maximum recorded lifespan for this species is 40 years [am = 40 years], a figure obtained from validated otolith readings of the oldest individuals recovered from the fishery. This remarkable longevity, when combined with a moderate age at first reproduction and high iteroparity, confers substantial demographic resilience to the population, buffering it against occasional years of poor recruitment. Older individuals, particularly those exceeding 30 years of age, have been observed to continue spawning annually, maintaining high fecundity even as somatic growth slows to a near halt. The trade-off between extended lifespan and delayed reproductive senescence is a recurring theme among large, temperate-reef serranids.
